title: A Turn Everyone Can See
bigQuestion: How do a whistle, a line, and a team size help people take fair turns?

story.title: The Whistle and the Line
story.kicker: A starter lifts a whistle. Shoes wait behind a white line.
paragraphs: On field day the starter stands beside a white line. Runners curl their toes behind it. No one may step over until the sound.
The starter blows a *whistle*. Eight children run. Eight more wait for the next heat. The wait is part of the race, not a punishment.
Later, in the gym, a soccer game uses another rule from the Laws of the Game. Each side may put eleven players on the pitch. Extra children wait as substitutes.
Ms. Ortiz says, "A turn you can see needs a mark and a signal. A team has a size written in a book, not just a feeling."
story.think: When did you wait so someone else could go first?

lessons.title: A Whistle Starts Many Games
lessons.mainIdea: Referees in soccer and basketball use a whistle so the whole room hears the same start or stop.
reading: In soccer, the referee carries a *whistle*. The Laws of the Game say the referee starts and stops play. The sound is for everyone on the pitch, not just one player.
Basketball officials use a whistle too. When the whistle blows, players are supposed to stop. One sound can reach a noisy gym.

words.d: a tool that makes a sharp sound to start or stop play
the official who starts and stops a soccer match

look.title: Who starts soccer play
look.text: The Laws of the Game give the referee power to start and stop play and to use a whistle so players and fans hear the same decision.
look.cite: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 5 (The Referee), current public summary of the referee's duties
look.prompt: Why does one person hold the whistle instead of every player?

check.q: Who starts and stops a soccer match?
check.why: The Laws of the Game give that job to the referee.

check.q: Why use a whistle in a gym?
choices: one sound can reach a noisy room
check.why: The reading says one sound can reach a noisy gym.

check.q: What should basketball players do when the whistle blows?
check.why: Officials use the whistle so players stop.

lessons.title: A Line You Must Not Cross Yet
lessons.mainIdea: Runners start from behind a line so every racer begins from the same place.
reading: On a track, runners wait behind a starting *line*. If someone steps over early, that is a false start. The race is not fair yet.
World Athletics races use starting blocks in many sprint events. The blocks hold the feet. The line still marks where the race begins.

words.d: the mark that shows where a race or turn begins

look.title: Toes behind the line
look.text: Look at eight pairs of shoes behind a white line. One shoe creeps over the paint. The starter raises a hand. That runner has left too soon.
look.prompt: Why does one early step make the race unfair?

check.why: They wait behind the starting line.
A false start is leaving before the signal.

check.q: What do many sprint races use to hold the feet?

lessons.title: Eleven on a Soccer Side
lessons.mainIdea: The Laws of the Game allow eleven players on each soccer team on the pitch.
reading: Soccer has a written team size. The Laws of the Game say each team may have eleven players on the *pitch*. One of them is the goalkeeper.
If more than eleven play at once, the extra person is not allowed. Substitutes wait off the pitch until a referee lets a change happen.

words.d: the rectangle where soccer is played
the player allowed to use the hands in the penalty area

look.title: Players on the pitch
rows: goalkeepers on the pitch at once
look.cite: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 3 (The Players): eleven players per team
look.prompt: How many players may one side have on the pitch?

check.q: How many soccer players may one team have on the pitch?
check.why: Law 3 allows eleven per team, including the goalkeeper.

check.q: Who may use the hands in the penalty area?

lessons.title: Five on a Basketball Side
lessons.mainIdea: A basketball team may have five players on the court at one time.
reading: Basketball uses a different number. Officials allow five players per team on the *court*. That number is in the playing rules, not just a habit.
Naismith's first game in 1891 used nine players on a side because his class was large. Later rules settled on five. Team size is written. It can change when a rule book changes.

words.d: the marked floor used for basketball

look.title: From nine to five
look.text: Naismith's first class in 1891 had eighteen students, so he used nine on a side. Later amateur and school rules set five players on the court for each team.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development (1941); NFHS / NCAA basketball rules on five players per team
look.prompt: What changed: the gym, or the written number?

check.q: How many basketball players may one team have on the court now?
check.why: Current playing rules allow five on the court.

check.q: How many were on a side in Naismith's first class game?
check.why: Eighteen students made nine on a side.

check.q: What can change a team size?
check.why: The reading says team size is written and can change with the book.

lessons.title: Both Sides Use the Same Words
lessons.mainIdea: Fair play means both sides hear and use the same written rule.
reading: A *fair* start uses one line and one signal for every racer. A fair soccer match uses the same Laws of the Game for both clubs.
If only one team knew the offside rule, the match would not be shared. Sharing a game means sharing the words in the book.

words.d: using the same rule for each side

look.title: One book, two sides
look.text: Two teams walk onto a pitch. The referee carries one rule book. Both captains hear the same start. No team gets a private whistle.
look.prompt: What would go wrong if each team used a different book?

choices: using the same rule for each side
check.why: Fair means the same rule for each side.

check.q: What do both soccer clubs use?
choices: the same Laws of the Game
check.why: Both sides use the same Laws of the Game.
The reading says sharing the words in the book.

lessons.title: Illinois Schools Use Shared Rules Too
lessons.mainIdea: The Illinois High School Association writes rules so schools in one state can meet.
reading: The *Illinois High School Association*, or IHSA, began in 1900. It runs state meets so schools can use shared rules.
IHSA boys wrestling state champions were first named in 1937. Those dates belong to school sport. They do not invent running or wrestling. They mark a state room.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, begun in 1900

look.title: A state meet date
look.text: The IHSA lists 1937 as the first year of a boys wrestling state championship. The association itself dates to 1900.
look.cite: Illinois High School Association records: IHSA founded 1900; boys wrestling state championship 1937
look.prompt: Which date marks the association, and which date marks one sport's state meet?

check.q: When were the first IHSA boys wrestling state champions named?

check.why: They mark Illinois school sport, not the invention of the games.

review.q: Who starts and stops a soccer match?
review.why: The referee holds that job under the Laws of the Game.
Leaving early is a false start.

review.q: How many soccer players may one team have on the pitch?
How many basketball players may one team have on the court now?

choices: each team writes its own book
both sides use the same rule
review.why: Fair means the same rule for each side.
